title: More weekly sets for a low-volume muscle
statement: In healthy adults training for muscle size (mostly young men, untrained or trained), more weekly sets per muscle give more muscle growth on average, but each extra set adds less than the one before. That supports raising a muscle from low volume (single sets, or under about 10 weekly sets) to about 10 weekly sets. Expect only a modest extra gain in size, with no promised strength benefit. Whether going above about 20 weekly sets adds anything more is uncertain.
population: Healthy adults doing resistance training to build muscle size. Most of the evidence comes from young men, both untrained and resistance-trained. Direct evidence in women, older adults and clinical groups was not verified, so the claim should not be presented as tested in those groups.
what_the_app_does: When a muscle gets fewer than 10 hard sets a week and you ask for it to grow, we can suggest adding sets toward 10, never above 20, within your session time.
supporting_source_ids: src-krieger-2010; src-schoenfeld-2017; src-pelland-2026; src-bernardez-vazquez-2022; src-schoenfeld-2019; src-radaelli-2015
verdict: Active. Six counted sources all point the same way: more volume gives more growth, with diminishing returns. They are the meta-analyses by Krieger 2010, Schoenfeld 2017 and Pelland 2026, the Bernárdez-Vázquez 2022 umbrella review, and the trials by Schoenfeld 2019 and Radaelli 2015. At least three of them come from independent research groups: Schoenfeld/Krieger, Pelland/Zourdos and Radaelli. The exact 10-set target comes from the umbrella review's conclusion and from the continuous dose-response models, not from a head-to-head trial. In Schoenfeld 2017 the under-10 versus 10+ category contrast was only a trend (P = 0.074). The main contrary result is Heaselgrave 2019: in trained men, 9 weekly biceps sets matched 18 or 27. But that trial covered one muscle over 6 weeks, mixed up volume with training frequency, and does not outweigh the pooled evidence. It, Baz-Valle 2022 and Schoenfeld 2019 (which favoured about 30+ sets) together leave the benefit above 20 sets uncertain.
evidence_gaps: 1. There is no head-to-head trial of about 5 to 9 versus 10 to 12 weekly sets per muscle, so the exact 10-set target rests on pooled trends and the umbrella review's conclusion. 2. Direct evidence in women, older adults and clinical groups was not verified. 3. These leads have not been checked yet: the ACSM 2026 position stand, Currier 2023 (the Br J Sports Med Bayesian network meta-analysis), Brigatto 2022 (PMID 31868813), Aubé 2022 (PMID 32058362) and Enes 2024 (PMID 37796222). If any of them showed no benefit from moving low volume up to about 10 sets, the status should be reconsidered. 4. No dedicated retraction check (for example Retraction Watch) was run on the eight sources, and the reportedly retracted Barbalho trials must not be used. 5. The effect above 20 weekly sets needs longer trials in trained people that do not mix up volume and frequency. Today those trials conflict: Schoenfeld 2019 against Heaselgrave 2019 and Baz-Valle 2022. 6. Several identifiers are still missing, such as the PMID for Bernárdez-Vázquez 2022. Most quotes were not seen word for word. 7. The strength outcome is mixed: Pelland 2026 found a positive slope with sharper diminishing returns, while Schoenfeld 2019 found no difference. The app should not claim any strength benefit from this claim.

title: Heavier loads for maximal strength
statement: In healthy adults, training with heavier loads (about 80% of 1RM or more, roughly 8 or fewer reps per set) gives larger gains in 1RM strength on the trained lifts than training with light loads (about 60% of 1RM or less, roughly 15 or more reps per set). An advantage over moderate loads (about 9-15 reps) is not established. When sets are taken to muscular failure, muscle growth is similar with light, moderate and heavy loads.
population: Healthy adults aged 18 and over. Most were young, untrained or recreationally trained, and more were men than women. The 1RM advantage of heavier loads was smaller in older adults (Refalo 2021: effect size 0.20 vs 0.34 in younger adults). Very few highly trained or elite athletes were studied, and the results in trained men are mixed: one RCT found load mostly did not change strength gains (Morton 2016), and a small RCT found larger squat gains with heavier loads (Schoenfeld 2015).
what_the_app_does: When you ask to get stronger, we can suggest heavier loads (about 8 reps or fewer) for main lifts you train with light loads (15 reps or more). We don't push lifts that are already moderate or heavy, because the evidence doesn't show that helps more.
supporting_source_ids: src-lopez-2021; src-currier-2023; src-refalo-2021; src-schoenfeld-2017-b; src-mcleod-2024; src-currier-2026; src-schoenfeld-2015
verdict: The narrowed claim is active. Seven counted sources support it, and five syntheses from at least four separate author groups agree that heavier loads give larger 1RM gains than light loads. These are Lopez 2021 and Currier 2023 (network meta-analyses), Refalo 2021 and Schoenfeld 2017 (pairwise meta-analyses) and Mcleod 2024 (umbrella review). The 2026 ACSM position stand and a small RCT (Schoenfeld 2015) back them up. The same syntheses find similar muscle growth across loads when sets go to failure. Morton 2016 runs against the strength half in trained men, and Hammert 2026 found the heavy-load edge on untested (isometric or isokinetic) strength inconclusive. Neither outweighs the pooled evidence, but they limit the claim to 1RM on the trained lifts. Lopez 2021 found moderate loads also beat light loads, so heavy over moderate, the specific 3-6 rep range, reps in reserve and rest lengths are not supported. The pairwise and network meta-analyses share many primary trials, and Currier 2023, Mcleod 2024 and ACSM 2026 come from overlapping McMaster authors, so the sources are less independent than their count suggests.
evidence_gaps: More evidence is needed in five areas. (1) Direct, volume-equated RCTs of heavy loads (about 3-6 reps) against moderate loads (about 8-12 reps), such as Mangine 2015 and Schoenfeld 2014 (not searched). These would be needed before the app could favour 3-6 reps over moderate loading. (2) Trials testing 2-3 reps in reserve and longer rests for strength. No verified source covers either, and the umbrella review found insufficient evidence on set end point and rest. (3) Evidence that similar growth across loads holds when sets stop short of failure. (4) More trials in trained and elite lifters, where results are mixed (Morton 2016 vs Schoenfeld 2015) and such lifters are about 2.3% of the evidence base. Also more trials in women and older adults, where the 1RM advantage looked smaller. (5) Better evidence on whether heavy-load gains carry over to strength tests that were not trained (Hammert 2026 was inconclusive). Several sources still need checking: Lopez 2021's effect sizes (high vs low SMD 0.60; high vs moderate non-significant) against its abstract or tables; ACSM 2026's PMID, abstract and hypertrophy recommendations; and the Currier 2023 and Mcleod 2024 identifiers on their own PubMed records. These leads were not verified or examined and were not used: Csapo & Alegre on older adults (PMID 26302881); the APNM volume-matched loads meta-analysis (doi 10.1139/apnm-2021-0515); the ACSM 2009 stand; the Schoenfeld 2016 Eur J Sport Sci meta-analysis (PMID 25530577); the 2026 paper on regional muscle and tendon growth (PMID 42319300), which may challenge similar growth in particular muscle regions; and a bioRxiv preprint. No dedicated retraction search was run for each paper.

title: Light or heavy loads grow muscle similarly
statement: In healthy young adults, training with loads from about 30% to about 85% of 1RM appears to give similar gains in whole-muscle size when sets are taken to momentary failure, while heavier loads still give larger gains in maximal (1RM) strength. This is not established for loads below about 30% of 1RM, or for light-load sets stopped well short of failure.
population: Healthy adults, untrained or resistance-trained. Most data come from young men aged about 18-35 in 6-12 week programmes. The claim is not established for women, older adults or highly trained athletes.
what_the_app_does: Would let us say that a change of load shouldn't cost you muscle. Until then, we don't say it.
context_source_ids: src-schoenfeld-2017-b; src-lopez-2021; src-refalo-2021; src-carvalho-2022; src-mcleod-2024; src-morton-2016; src-lees-2026; src-mitchell-2012; src-grgic-2020; src-lasevicius-2018
verdict: No source counts toward this claim. Verification of all 15 sources stopped when the shared web-search budget ran out, so no abstract or finding was checked against the claim, and every design, direction and finding check is unknown. The candidate evidence looks consistent: meta-analyses from four groups (Schoenfeld 2017, Lopez 2021, Refalo 2021, Carvalho 2022) and trials such as Mitchell 2012, Morton 2016 and Lees all report similar growth across loads. But the app's 3-source rule cannot be met until at least three of them pass verification. Even then the claim has limits: 20% 1RM gave about half the growth of 80% (Lasevicius 2018); light-load sets stopped short of failure appear to give less growth (Lasevicius 2022, identity not yet confirmed); fibre-level data lean non-significantly towards heavy loads (Grgic 2020); and heavier loads consistently give larger strength gains.
evidence_gaps: The decisive gap is verification, not evidence. Re-run verification in a turn with search budget available. At least three of Schoenfeld 2017, Lopez 2021, Refalo 2021, Carvalho 2022, Morton 2016, Lees and Mitchell 2012 must pass every check (identifier, metadata on a second independent page, peer review, retraction status, strong design, and a finding that supports the claim) before the status can be active. Because the meta-analyses share most of their primary trials, and Mitchell, Morton and Lees come from one laboratory, the counted set should include reviews from different groups, or at least one RCT from another laboratory (e.g. Schoenfeld 2015), so the agreement is not the same data counted twice. Lasevicius 2022 needs its identity confirmed to support the rule that light-load sets must end at or within about 1 rep of failure, and direct trials of light loads at 1-3 reps in reserve would be needed to extend the claim from 'to failure' to 'close to failure'. Lasevicius 2018 should be verified to fix the lower bound at about 30% 1RM. The upper bound above about 85-90% 1RM rests only on a small 2025 trial (Cumming et al.) with an unconfirmed PMID. Applying the claim beyond young men would need trials in women, older adults and highly trained athletes. The type II fibre question (Grgic 2020) remains open.

title: Spreading the same sets over more days
statement: In healthy adults, when weekly sets per muscle are kept the same, training a muscle once a week or spreading those sets over two or three sessions a week appears to give similar muscle growth. This has not yet been confirmed by verified sources, and no claim is made about strength.
population: Healthy adults, mostly young (pooled mean age about 25) and mostly male (about 79%), untrained or resistance-trained, doing supervised programmes of about 6 to 12 weeks (some up to about 30) at 1 to 3 sessions per muscle per week. The evidence does not reliably cover women, adults over 60, clinical groups, more than 3 sessions per muscle per week, or programmes much longer than 12 weeks.
what_the_app_does: Would let us move sets between days to fit your session time. Until then, we only move them when you edit your plan.
verdict: None of the nine candidate sources counts: the shared search budget ran out before any checks ran, so for every source the identity, peer-review status, retraction status, design and reported finding are all unknown. The submitted evidence looks consistent for hypertrophy (Schoenfeld 2019, Pelland 2026, Tao 2026, Ramos-Campo 2024 and Pedersen 2024 all report no meaningful difference at equal volume), but none of it is verified, so the claim must stay a draft. Two sources point the other way: Schoenfeld 2016 found twice a week beat once a week, and the small Zaroni 2019 trial found more growth with 5 sessions a week. Both favour more frequent training, so they do not suggest splitting sets would cause harm. The strength part, including the 'mainly through extra volume' clause, is contested: Grgic 2018 and Cuthbert 2021 found no volume-equated effect, while Tao 2026, Pelland 2026 and Pedersen 2024 report a small independent benefit. So it is left out of the statement.
evidence_gaps: 1) Verification has to be re-run, ideally in a turn with search budget left. At least 3 of Schoenfeld 2019, Pelland 2026, Tao 2026, Ramos-Campo 2024 and Pedersen 2024 must pass every check (identifier, metadata, peer review, no retraction, strong design) with a confirmed volume-equated hypertrophy finding. Specific items to resolve: the Grgic 2018 PMID conflict (29470825 vs 28444646), the journal and peer-review status of Tao 2026, the full citation for Pelland 2026, and whether every trial in Ramos-Campo 2024 equated volume. 2) The volume-equated RCTs the researcher cited (Hamarsland 2022, Gomes 2019, Saric 2019, Gentil 2018, Brigatto 2019) were never put forward for verification. Verifying them would add primary evidence that does not rely on overlapping meta-analyses. 3) Even once verified, the meta-analyses draw on the same pool of small trials and often share authors. At least one source from an independent group, or independent primary trials, would strengthen any activation. 4) Supporting 4 or more sessions per muscle per week would need more volume-equated trials at those frequencies. 5) Trials in women, adults over 60, clinical groups, and programmes longer than 12 weeks are needed before the claim can be extended to them. 6) A strength statement would need agreement between Grgic 2018 and Cuthbert 2021 on one side and Tao 2026, Pelland 2026 and Pedersen 2024 on the other. The question is whether frequency helps strength independently of volume or through extra practice of the tested lift. 7) No source gives a maximum number of sets per session, so the app has no basis for a per-session cap.

title: Stopping sets short of failure
statement: In healthy, mostly young adults, training to failure is not needed: stopping sets short of failure gives similar, and sometimes slightly greater, strength gains, and similar or only slightly smaller muscle growth. For muscle growth, ending sets closer to failure tends to give a little more growth; for strength, how close to failure sets end matters little.
population: Healthy adults, mostly young (about 18 to 35), both untrained and resistance-trained, in supervised programmes lasting roughly 6 to 14 weeks. Evidence in older adults and in highly trained or elite lifters is limited.
what_the_app_does: Explains why our plans never ask you to train to failure: stopping a little short works about as well.
verdict: Four counted sources support the narrowed claim. For strength, Grgic 2022, Davies 2016 and Robinson 2024 agree that stopping short of failure gives similar or slightly better gains. For muscle growth, Grgic 2022, Refalo 2023 and Robinson 2024 agree that failure gives at most a small advantage, and Robinson finds growth rises as sets end closer to failure. The main contrary evidence is Vieira 2021, which found a moderate growth advantage for failure (SMD 0.75); that advantage disappears when training volumes are matched, and it does not outweigh the larger, later analyses. The draft's '1 to 3 reps in reserve' range and the researcher's '0 to 2 RIR, 3 at most' limits are not set by any counted source, so those numbers are dropped. The reviews also share many of the same small, short trials, so they are less independent than four sources suggests.
evidence_gaps: 1. Specific reps-in-reserve targets need at least three counted sources that test or estimate outcomes at defined RIR values. Examples are head-to-head trials of about 1 to 3 RIR against failure for growth, or verified per-RIR predictions from the Robinson 2024 full text. No trial yet compares 3 RIR directly with 0 RIR for growth. 2. Verifying the Wu 2026 metadata (authors, volume, PMID) would add a fourth independent-analysis source for strength and growth. 3. Checking that limbs were randomly allocated in Refalo 2024 would let that trial count for the 1 to 2 RIR finding. 4. The content of the Davies 2016 erratum and of the comment on Refalo 2023 is unknown. 5. The reviews share many of the same primary trials, and Robinson 2024 shares authors and data with Refalo 2023. Independent, larger and longer trials (over 12 weeks) with measured rather than estimated RIR would strengthen the evidence. 6. Evidence is sparse for older adults and for highly trained or elite lifters, so the statement should not be extended to them without dedicated studies. 7. No dedicated retraction-database search was run.

title: Longer rests between sets
statement: When the number of sets stays the same, resting more than about 60 seconds between sets may give slightly more muscle growth than resting 60 seconds or less. There seems to be no clear extra benefit beyond about 90 seconds, and the difference is small and uncertain. For strength, resistance-trained lifters gain more with rests longer than about 2 minutes, while untrained people do about as well with 60-120 seconds.
population: Healthy adults doing resistance training, mostly young men. The finding that rests over 2 minutes help strength applies only to resistance-trained lifters. For untrained people, 60-120 seconds appears to be enough for strength. The evidence covers exercises in general and has nothing specific to multi-joint lifts. Women, older adults and programmes longer than about 10-12 weeks are barely represented.
what_the_app_does: Would let us suggest rest times between sets. Until then, your rests are whatever your plan says, and we use them only to estimate session length.
verdict: Draft. Only three sources pass every check (Singer 2024, Grgic 2018 and Schoenfeld 2016), and each backs a different part of the claim. Muscle growth is supported only by Singer 2024 (small effect, credible intervals crossing zero) and Schoenfeld 2016. Strength in trained lifters is supported only by Grgic 2018 and Schoenfeld 2016. So no single statement has three counted sources, and the Schoenfeld trial probably also sits inside both reviews, which share an author. The original draft's claim that 2 minutes or more gives more growth is not supported beyond about 90 seconds, and nothing isolates multi-joint lifts. Volume-matched trials (Longo 2022, Attarieh 2026) suggest any advantage comes from the extra volume that longer rests allow. Fink 2018 found the opposite, but rest was confounded with load. The ACSM 2026 stand reportedly found no strength effect of rest, but that is unverified.
evidence_gaps: The status could change to active if each part of the statement had at least 3 counted, reasonably independent sources. For muscle growth, a further strong source is needed. The status could change if randomisation is confirmed in Buresh 2009, if the Grgic 2017 abstract wording on trained participants is checked, or if a new well-powered randomised trial or independent meta-analysis with sets held equal is found. For strength in trained lifters, the lead PMID 19811949 (1, 3 and 5-minute rests in trained men) should be verified, along with any other independent randomised trial. The study lists of Singer 2024 and Grgic 2017/2018 need to be compared to see how far they reuse the same trials, including Schoenfeld 2016. The primary text of the ACSM 2026 stand must be checked: if it reports no effect of rest on strength, that would weigh against the claim. The following checks are still to do: the Attarieh 2026 correction, randomisation in Longo 2022, and dedicated retraction searches. No study compares multi-joint with single-joint exercises, so the draft's multi-joint wording cannot be tested. Data on women, older adults and training longer than about 12 weeks are needed before the claim is applied to those users.

title: Strength training on 2 or more days a week
statement: Not yet verified: WHO (2020) and US (2018) guidelines are reported to recommend that adults do muscle-strengthening activity on 2 or more days a week, alongside aerobic activity, and observational studies are reported to link any such activity with lower all-cause mortality. None of the sources has been verified, so this stays a draft and the app changes nothing.
population: Adults aged 18 and over in the general, non-clinical population. This is the proposed scope and has not been verified. The guideline part would cover adults aged 18 to 64 and those aged 65 and over. The mortality evidence would come mostly from middle-aged and older adults in prospective cohorts.
what_the_app_does: Would let us suggest a second strength day for the general health goal.
verdict: No source counts towards this claim. The shared web-search budget ran out before any check could run, so all 9 sources, including the two guidelines (Bull 2020, Piercy 2018) and the main meta-analyses (Momma 2022, Shailendra 2022, Saeidifard 2019), have every check marked unknown. With zero of the 3 required sources verified, the claim stays a draft, however plausible it is. Even the researcher's own description of the evidence would narrow the claim. It shows null or borderline results for cancer and cardiovascular mortality (Saeidifard 2019; Nascimento 2021 high vs low HR 0.87, 0.73-1.02), J- or U-shaped dose curves, no hard-outcome trials and heavy overlap between the meta-analyses.
evidence_gaps: 1) Verification has to run before anything else. At least 3 sources must pass every check (identifier, metadata, peer review, not retracted, strong design, finding supported) with the direction 'supports'. Re-check the most likely ones first: Bull 2020 (WHO) and Piercy 2018 (US PAG) for the 2-days-a-week recommendation, then Momma 2022, Shailendra 2022 and Saeidifard 2019 for the mortality link. Confirm the Shailendra PMID (35599175 vs 36528354) and look for retraction or correction notices on all of them. 2) Even if these pass, the statement probably needs narrowing. On the reported findings, the evidence is strongest for the guideline recommendation and for lower all-cause mortality. It is weak or null for total cancer mortality (Nascimento high vs low; Saeidifard) and borderline for cardiovascular mortality, so 'chronic disease' should not be stated without qualification. 3) The meta-analyses probably pool many of the same cohorts, and the guidelines draw on the same evidence base. A check of study-by-study overlap is needed before treating them as independent. 4) The pooled dose-response data is in minutes per week, not days per week. Direct evidence that 2 or more days beats 1 day exists only for total cancer mortality (Nascimento, HR 0.81), so the 2-day threshold rests on guideline consensus. 5) All hard-outcome evidence is observational and self-reported. Randomised trials, or well-controlled cohorts with device-measured activity, would be needed to support any causal framing. 6) The dose ceiling is uncertain: the reported peak is 30-60 min/week in Momma and about 60 min/week in Shailendra, against a plateau above 120 min/week in Zhang 2026. This needs resolving before the app sets any volume figure.

title: Planned lighter weeks
statement: Not established: there is no verified evidence that planned deload weeks improve strength or muscle gains compared with continuous resistance training.
population: Healthy adults doing resistance training. The trials, none of them verified yet, mostly studied untrained or detrained young adults. Only one studied resistance-trained adults (39 people). There are no data for older adults or competitive athletes, and none beyond 6 months.
what_the_app_does: Would let us suggest planned lighter (deload) weeks. Until then, we never add them.
context_source_ids: src-coleman-2024; src-pancar-2026; src-halonen-2024; src-ogasawara-2013; src-ogasawara-2011; src-gentil-2015; src-bosquet-2013; src-bell-2023; src-rogerson-2024
verdict: Draft: no source passed verification. The web search budget ran out before any identifier, metadata, retraction or design check could run, so 0 sources count against the 3 required. Even taken at face value, none of the reported trials shows a benefit, so the draft claim that deloads "improve" gains would fail anyway. The direct trials are Coleman 2024 and Pancar 2026. The break-versus-continuous trials are Ogasawara 2011 and 2013, Gentil 2015 and Halonen 2024. All report similar overall gains, and Coleman 2024 reports somewhat smaller lower-body strength gains after a full week off. The researcher's narrower "little or no cost, no benefit" statement cannot be activated until at least three of these trials pass verification. Coleman 2024's direction label is also inconsistent: it is labelled as contradicting, but its finding supports the narrower statement, so it needs rechecking.
evidence_gaps: Before any deload statement can become active, at least three trials must pass every check: PMID or DOI, metadata, peer review, retraction status, randomised design, and that the reported findings match the paper. The best candidates are Coleman 2024 (PMID 38274324 / PMC10809978), Pancar 2026 (a published record must first be found), Halonen 2024, Ogasawara 2013 and Gentil 2015. Ogasawara 2011 also needs its randomisation confirmed. Supporting the original claim that deloads improve gains would take something much stronger: randomised trials in resistance-trained lifters showing that roughly one-week reduced-volume deloads produce larger strength or muscle gains than continuous training, ideally pooled in a systematic review. Those trials would also need follow-up beyond 6 months and outcomes such as injury, overreaching and adherence. Registered trials NCT06825052 and NCT06573086 (TraDeRe2024) may help fill this gap.

title: Adding cardio to strength training
statement: Adding aerobic training to resistance training does not meaningfully reduce muscle growth or maximal strength, though it may blunt explosive strength.
what_the_app_does: Would let us add runs without cutting your lifting.
verdict: We have not finished checking the evidence for this claim, so the app treats it as unsupported and changes nothing.

title: Limiting weekly running increases
statement: A gradual weekly distance progression (for example no more than 10% a week) reduces running injuries.
what_the_app_does: Would let us limit how fast your weekly running distance rises. Until then, we don't plan your running.
verdict: We have not finished checking the evidence for this claim, so the app treats it as unsupported and changes nothing.

title: Lifting less on low-HRV days
statement: Lowering lifting volume on days of low HRV improves results.
what_the_app_does: Would let a low readiness reduce today's lifting. Until then, readiness never changes your plan; we show it so you can decide.
verdict: We have not finished checking the evidence for this claim, so the app treats it as unsupported and changes nothing.

title: HRV-guided endurance training
statement: Adjusting endurance training day to day based on HRV gives similar or slightly better fitness and performance gains than a fixed plan.
what_the_app_does: Would let us swap a hard run for an easy one on a low-HRV day. Until then, readiness never changes your plan.
verdict: We have not finished checking the evidence for this claim, so the app treats it as unsupported and changes nothing.

title: Short sleep and next-day performance
statement: In healthy adults and athletes tested in the lab, one night of restricted or no sleep lowers physical performance the next day on average, including aerobic endurance. How much it drops varies widely between studies and tasks, so the average cannot predict the effect for any one person.
population: Healthy adults and athletes, mostly young men, tested in laboratory randomised or crossover studies the day after one night (about 24 h) of no sleep or partly restricted sleep. It does not cover several nights of short sleep in a row, habitual short sleepers or sleep tracked in everyday life. Evidence on women and older adults is limited.
what_the_app_does: Explains your readiness: short sleep can make a session feel harder. It never changes your plan by itself.
verdict: Active, in a narrowed form. Three verified meta-analyses from different teams (Craven 2022, Gong 2024 and Kong 2025) all find that one night of sleep loss lowers next-day physical performance on average, and all three show it for aerobic endurance. Craven puts the average drop at about 7.6%, but heterogeneity is extreme (I² about 98%) and the other two report only standardised effect sizes, so no percentage is carried into the app. Several of the researcher's details are left out because they rest on one source or on subgroup figures nobody verified, and Kong's summary partly conflicts with some of them: the 6 h threshold, the "feels harder" (RPE) wording, strength falling "only after total deprivation", early-night restriction having no effect, and the time-of-day and late-restriction moderators, which only two counted sources back. Knowles 2018 and Easow 2025 show that strength effects are mixed but do not contradict the overall direction. Because the three meta-analyses share many primary trials, the app should use this only to explain, never to change the plan.
evidence_gaps: 1) Any hours threshold (for example "6 h or less") needs checking against the Craven full text or another counted source before the app ties the message to a number. 2) To add timing or protocol detail (worse in afternoon or evening, worse after waking early, weaker after going to bed late), a third counted source has to confirm it. Kong's subgroup results by type of sleep loss and Gong's per-protocol figures (including the reportedly small -0.23 for a full night without sleep) must be verified, and the conflict over early-night restriction resolved. 3) To mention strength or perceived effort, the Craven strength subgroup (about -3%, total deprivation only, lower body) and Kong's RPE result (SMD 0.47) need verification against the full text. 4) Showing users a percentage would need at least three sources reporting comparable percentage effects; only Craven does. 5) The three meta-analyses share many of the same small lab crossover trials. An overlap check, or large independent trials, would show how independent they really are; if they turn out to rest on the same handful of trials, the status should be reconsidered. 6) The population cannot be widened without evidence on women, older adults, habitual short sleepers, real-world sleep tracked by wearables, and whether caffeine or naps offset the effect. 7) Several sources are still unverified and were not used: the endurance-specific meta-analysis seen on ResearchGate, Bonnar 2018, the Heliyon 2024 trial in Sanda athletes (mixed results), and PMID 41900490 on sex differences. Knowles 2018's PMID is also unconfirmed. Large new trials or meta-analyses finding no effect after one night would also call for a review.

title: How accurate wearables are
statement: In healthy, mostly young adults at rest, heart rate variability (HRV) from consumer and portable devices is close to ECG-measured HRV but not the same. The error is small but real and varies with the device, the HRV metric and body position, so readings should not be treated as interchangeable with ECG values, with other devices or with other metrics. Against polysomnography, consumer sleep trackers detect sleep well but miss much of the time spent awake, and their sleep-stage and sleep-summary estimates (such as total sleep time and wake after sleep onset) differ meaningfully.
population: Healthy, mostly young adults (roughly 18-40) using consumer wrist, ring, strap or app-based devices. The HRV evidence comes mainly from resting measurements; among the counted sources, only one single-night laboratory study (Miller 2022) has night-time data. The sleep evidence comes mainly from laboratory comparisons with polysomnography. The claim is not established for older adults, clinical populations (where agreement appears worse), exercise, or free-living daytime measurement.
what_the_app_does: Explains why we compare each device only with its own baseline and keep each maker's score under its own name.
supporting_source_ids: src-miller-2022; src-dobbs-2019; src-xu-2026; src-stone-2021; src-chinoy-2021; src-lee-2025; src-schyvens-2024
verdict: Active, but only for a narrowed, explanatory statement. Four counted sources agree that wearable HRV is close to ECG HRV but not equivalent, with an error that varies: the Dobbs 2019 and Xu 2026 meta-analyses, Stone 2021 and Miller 2022. Four more agree that sleep-versus-wake detection is reasonable but that wake detection, sleep stages and sleep-summary metrics differ from polysomnography: Miller 2022, Chinoy 2021, Lee 2025 and Schyvens 2024. Some parts of the proposed statement were dropped because they rest mainly on Dial 2025 (not counted, rated mixed) and on unverified Miller figures: the night-time resting heart rate accuracy, the device rankings (Oura/WHOOP good, Polar/Garmin poor) and the numeric HR/HRV error ranges. The tensions in the evidence do not undermine the conservative within-device, labelled-value use. Dobbs found no device-type effect, and Dobbs and Xu disagree on which metric has the larger error. Kantrowitz 2025 found worse agreement in clinical patients, which fits the statement rather than contradicting it.
evidence_gaps: The following evidence is needed before the claim can go further. (1) At least three counted, independent ECG-referenced studies of night-time resting heart rate in current consumer wearables; only Miller's WHOOP data is verified now, and Dial 2025 was not counted. These would be needed before stating heart rate accuracy or any '1-2 bpm' figure. (2) Larger night-time HRV validations: Xu 2026 warns against generalising resting results to sleep, and the 5-8% RMSSD error figure rests on Dial 2025 (n=13) alone. (3) A direct test of cross-device interchangeability, measuring the same people on the same nights with several devices and comparing the devices with one another; this is currently inferred from device-specific error against ECG. (4) Independent replication of device rankings (Oura/WHOOP good, Polar/Garmin poor) across current device generations, free of manufacturer involvement, and checks of Miller's unverified Oura and Polar figures. (5) A resolution of the inconsistencies: Dobbs found no device-type effect while Stone and Dial found large device differences, and Dobbs and Xu disagree on whether SDNN or RMSSD has the larger error. (6) Evidence in older adults, clinical populations, during exercise and in free-living use. (7) More verified sleep-stage accuracy data beyond Miller's 50-65% and Schyvens' qualitative review; for example, the uncaptured npj Digital Medicine 2024 staging paper and the 2025 six-device validation. (8) Formal retraction and expression-of-concern checks for every source, especially Xu 2026, and a check for overlapping studies between the reviews and the primary studies.

title: Protein for muscle gain
statement: For healthy adults doing resistance training for at least 6 weeks, a total protein intake of about 1.6 g per kg of body weight per day appears, on average, to be enough to get the extra muscle-mass gain that protein can add, and intakes of 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg/day are generally sufficient. The extra gain from protein is small, around 0.3 kg of fat-free mass on average in pooled trials.
population: Healthy, non-obese adults who do structured resistance training for at least 6 weeks to gain muscle, and who are not cutting calories. The benefit is smaller in older adults, and the evidence for them is less consistent. It does not cover people cutting calories (the ISSN suggests 2.3 to 3.1 g/kg/day to keep lean mass during a calorie deficit), pregnant people, or people with medical conditions such as kidney disease.
what_the_app_does: Would let us suggest a protein target for muscle gain. Until then, your targets are yours to set.
verdict: This stays a draft because only two sources count: Morton 2018 (the main finding is a meta-regression breakpoint at about 1.6 g/kg/day, with an extra 0.30 kg of fat-free mass) and the 2017 ISSN position stand by Jäger (1.4 to 2.0 g/kg/day is sufficient). The rule needs three. Bagheri 2023 would back 1.6 g/kg/day as enough for trained young men, but it was not counted because the text seen never says participants were randomised. Nunes 2022 was not counted either: it is mixed, and its age-group results were not verified. The counted sources do not support the proposed 2.2 g/kg/day cap: the confidence interval behind it comes from a later review, and the ISSN upper bound is 2.0. They also do not support the claim that 3.2 g/kg/day adds nothing, which rests only on Bagheri. Tagawa 2021 points the other way: lean-mass gains slowed above about 1.3 g/kg/day but did not stop, so the evidence shows diminishing returns rather than a firm ceiling at 1.6.
evidence_gaps:
- A third counted source. The quickest route is to confirm in the Bagheri 2023 methods (PMC10388821) that participants were randomised. If they were, it would count, but only for trained young men, and only to show that 1.6 g/kg/day is enough compared with 3.2.
- Verification of the Nunes 2022 subgroup results: the under-65 vs 65-and-over split, the benefit at 1.2 to 1.59 g/kg/day in older adults, and the effect sizes, plus a check that its strength CI is a reporting error.
- Randomised trials in trained adults with muscle size as the outcome that compare 1.6 with 2.2 g/kg/day, and 1.2 with 1.6 g/kg/day. These are needed to support any upper cap above 2.0 or any statement that higher intakes add nothing.
- Direct verification of the Morton 2018 breakpoint from the full text: the 1.62 figure, its 95% CI of about 1.03 to 2.20, the p-value and the number of study arms. Also confirmation of what the 2020 correction changed.
- A reconciliation of Tagawa 2021's continuing slope above 1.3 g/kg/day with the plateau idea, for example a dose-response analysis limited to people doing resistance training.
- Longer trials that measure muscle size directly rather than fat-free mass by DXA or BIA, and better evidence for older adults and untrained people.
- Dedicated retraction checks (for example Retraction Watch) for Bagheri, Nunes and Tagawa.
- Safety evidence for higher intakes in people with medical conditions or who are pregnant.

title: Daily fibre
statement: In prospective studies of generally healthy adults, people who eat more dietary fibre from food have lower rates of cardiovascular disease (including coronary heart disease) and colorectal cancer. The risk is about 9% lower for cardiovascular and coronary disease for each extra 7 g a day, and about 10% lower for colorectal cancer for each extra 10 g a day, and the largest review found the biggest risk reductions at about 25 to 29 g a day. These are associations, not proven cause and effect, and any extra benefit above about 30 g a day is uncertain.
population: Generally healthy adults in general-population prospective cohorts, mostly in high-income countries. This is not evidence for children (EFSA uses a separate value of 2 g/MJ for children aged 1 and over). It is also not evidence for preventing new polyps or bowel cancer in people who have already had colorectal adenomas, or for fibre supplements used in place of fibre from food.
what_the_app_does: If your fibre target is under 25 g a day, we can suggest 25 to 30 g. It also explains the fibre line in food ratings.
supporting_source_ids: src-reynolds-2019; src-threapleton-2013; src-aune-2011; src-interact-consortium-2015; src-veronese-2025; src-veettil-2021; src-hartley-2016
verdict: The status is active, but the statement is narrower than the draft. Seven counted sources agree that eating more fibre is linked to lower risk. For cardiovascular and coronary disease the decisive sources are Threapleton 2013, Reynolds 2019 and Veronese 2025; for colorectal cancer they are Aune 2011, Reynolds 2019 and Veettil 2021. Hartley 2016 adds short trials showing modest falls in cholesterol and diastolic blood pressure. The 25 to 29 g/day sweet spot comes from Reynolds alone, so the app uses 25 g/day only as a modest minimum, which the per-gram dose-response results also support. Several parts of the draft were removed or softened: "greater benefit at higher intakes", the causal framing, and the links to all-cause death and type 2 diabetes. Each of those links has only two counted sources, and the diabetes link lost significance after adjusting for body weight in InterAct 2015. The Cochrane trials in people with prior polyps (Yao 2017) found no fall in adenoma recurrence and a low-quality signal of more cancer diagnoses with fibre. Those trials studied a different population, so they do not outweigh the cohort evidence in healthy adults.
evidence_gaps:
1. No randomised trial has tested fibre intake against hard outcomes (death, cardiovascular events, type 2 diabetes or colorectal cancer incidence). The links to disease and death are observational and open to confounding by overall diet quality, body weight and lifestyle, and to error in food-frequency measurement. A long-term trial with hard outcomes, or strong Mendelian randomisation evidence, would be needed before the app makes causal claims.
2. The 25 to 29 g/day point of greatest risk reduction rests on one counted source (Reynolds 2019). A second and third verified dose-response analysis locating the lowest risk would firm up the specific target. EFSA's 25 g/day is based on bowel function and is not counted, and the WHO 2023 guideline was seen only in secondary reports.
3. Lower all-cause mortality (Reynolds 2019, Veronese 2025) and lower type 2 diabetes risk (Reynolds 2019, InterAct 2015) each have only two counted sources. The diabetes link also weakens after adjusting for body weight. Adding these to the statement and health rating would need a third verified source each, for example a corrected Yao 2023 entry or a verified Ramezani 2024 (Clin Nutr 43(1):65-83), and the all-cause figure of 0.90 per 10 g/day would need a counted source (Yang 2015 was seen only in passing).
4. Whether benefit continues above about 30 g/day is uncertain. Few participants eat that much, and Yao 2023 (not counted) reported a non-linear all-cause curve.
5. The counted meta-analyses and umbrella reviews pool largely the same cohorts, so they are not independent replications.
6. Colorectal evidence conflicts by population. Cohorts support a lower risk, but trials in people with prior polyps (Yao 2017 Cochrane) found no benefit and a low-quality signal of more cancer diagnoses. Larger, longer trials would clarify this.
7. Still unverified: what the Reynolds 2019 Department of Error corrects; the PMID, full author list and type 2 diabetes and colorectal grades of Veronese 2025; the Veettil fibre effect size (RR 0.84); and some identifiers (PMID 33591366 for Veettil, PMC6465195 for Yao 2017).
8. Most data come from adults in high-income countries, and fibre definitions differ between studies (AOAC methods vs non-starch polysaccharide), so gram amounts are not always comparable.

title: Protein and kidney function
statement: In adults with healthy kidneys, higher protein intakes do not harm kidney function; people with kidney disease need individual advice.
what_the_app_does: Would explain whether higher protein is safe for healthy kidneys. Until then, we don't suggest raising protein.
verdict: We have not finished checking the evidence for this claim, so the app treats it as unsupported and changes nothing.

title: Free sugars
statement: Higher free sugar intake is linked to worse health, though most evidence beyond weight and tooth decay is observational and low quality. In adults on unrestricted diets, cutting free sugars lowers weight only slightly (about 0.8 kg on average, through eating fewer calories overall), and keeping free sugars below 10% of daily energy is linked to less tooth decay (moderate-quality evidence).
population: Weight effect: adults on unrestricted (ad libitum) diets. Trials in children showed no overall weight change. Tooth decay (caries) link: children and adults. The wider links to disease come mostly from observational studies in general populations.
what_the_app_does: Explains the sugar line in food ratings.
verdict: Active, but narrowed. Four counted sources agree in direction. Te Morenga 2013 found about 0.8 kg less weight in adults on unrestricted diets, explained by lower calorie intake, with no overall effect in children. Moynihan & Kelly 2014 and its update Moores 2022 found moderate-quality evidence of less tooth decay below 10% of energy. The Huang 2023 umbrella review found mostly harmful associations, largely from low-quality observational data. The support is less independent than the count of four suggests: Moores updates Moynihan with overlapping data, Huang pools earlier meta-analyses, and the weight figure rests on one meta-analysis. So the statement stays modest and leaves out the WHO recommendation (not a peer-reviewed journal source) and the 5% target (low or very-low-quality evidence). Erickson 2017 (industry-funded) and Yan 2022 (a narrative review) question how strong the guideline evidence is, but they do not reverse the direction of effect, so they do not outweigh the counted sources.
evidence_gaps:
The active status rests on few independent bodies of evidence: one trial meta-analysis for weight (Te Morenga 2013) and, for tooth decay, one review plus its own non-independent update (Moynihan 2014, Moores 2022). Huang 2023 largely re-pools earlier work. The following would strengthen or test the claim:
(1) A recent independent or Cochrane meta-analysis of randomised trials on free sugars and body weight, ideally separating sugars in drinks from sugars in solid food. This would test Yan 2022's argument directly.
(2) An independent caries review, or causal evidence. The Mendelian randomisation study (PMID 41430990) found no strong evidence that genetically predicted sugar intake causes caries. Its journal and year need confirming and it should be properly assessed, because a robust null result would weaken the caries element.
(3) Missing details: Malik 2013's pooled effect sizes and Moores 2022's PMID. A dedicated Retraction Watch check was not run for each paper, although title searches found no retraction notices.
What would change the claim:
- Adding the WHO under-10% recommendation to the statement would need a peer-reviewed source that states it.
- Presenting the under-5% target as evidence-backed would need moderate-quality or better evidence.
- The status should return to draft if an independent high-quality review or strong causal evidence found no weight or caries benefit from keeping free sugars below 10% of energy.

title: Salt and blood pressure
statement: Eating less salt lowers blood pressure on average in adults. In pooled randomised trials, systolic pressure fell by about 3 to 4 mm Hg.
population: Adults in randomised trials, mostly in high-income countries, including people with and without high blood pressure. The statement does not give a separate effect for people with normal blood pressure. It has not been verified for children or for people with chronic kidney disease.
what_the_app_does: Explains the salt line in food ratings.
verdict: Three verified BMJ meta-analyses of randomised trials (He 2013, Huang 2020 and Aburto 2013) agree that eating less salt lowers blood pressure in adults. Their pooled systolic falls are about 3.4 to 4.3 mm Hg, so this narrowed statement is active for explanatory use. Only two counted reviews (He 2013 and Huang 2020) back the researcher's split by blood pressure status and the dose-response finding. Aburto 2013 did not confirm the split, and the older Midgley 1996 analysis found only about 1.0/0.1 mm Hg per 100 mmol in trials of people with normal blood pressure, so the claim and its size for people without high blood pressure stay out of the active statement. The three reviews pool overlapping trials and results vary a lot between trials (I² up to 75%). No evidence against lower blood pressure was seen, but the Graudal Cochrane review, the main source arguing the effect is small, was not checked.
evidence_gaps:
1. To say the effect holds for people with normal blood pressure, and to give separate sizes for people with and without high blood pressure, the app needs a third verified source with results for people with normal blood pressure. Candidates are the Graudal Cochrane review (low- vs high-sodium diet), Filippini 2021 (Circulation, dose-response) and the DASH-Sodium trial (Sacks 2001, NEJM). The Graudal review must be checked either way, because it is the strongest likely mixed or contradicting source.
2. The dose-response figure (about 1.1 mm Hg per 50 mmol) and the claim that longer trials show bigger effects each need a third verified source, such as Filippini 2021 or Gupta 2023 (JAMA crossover trial).
3. Children, people with chronic kidney disease and populations in low- and middle-income countries are not covered. The children's meta-analysis (IJE 2018) was dropped as unverified.
4. Effects on heart attack, stroke or death, including the J-curve debate about very low sodium, were not assessed. Any app claim about these needs separate evidence.
5. A numeric salt target needs peer-reviewed support. The WHO under 5 g salt a day target was seen only on a web page that is not peer-reviewed, and He 2013's 3 g target was not verified.
6. Mizuta 2025 (Hypertension Research) needs its identifier, metadata and retraction status verified.
7. Huang 2020's PMID, Aburto 2013's PMCID and participant counts, and some confidence intervals were not confirmed.
8. Dedicated retraction searches were limited.
9. The three counted reviews pool overlapping trials, so a fully independent confirmation, such as a large well-run trial, would strengthen the claim.

title: Saturated fat and heart disease
statement: Not yet verified: in adults, replacing saturated fat with polyunsaturated fat (vegetable oils, nuts, seeds) for at least 2 years may modestly lower the risk of cardiovascular events, but cutting saturated fat has not been shown to help people live longer.
population: Adults, mostly middle-aged, with or without existing cardiovascular disease, in trials lasting at least 2 years (many older trials enrolled mostly men). Any benefit is expected to be larger in absolute terms for people at higher cardiovascular risk. Not established for children or for mortality outcomes. Applies to no one in the app until the sources are verified.
what_the_app_does: Would explain why saturated fat is on the food rating.
verdict: None of the nine sources could be verified: the shared web search budget was used up before any check ran, so no source counts towards the claim and the status has to stay draft. If the proposed supporting sources are confirmed, they would back a narrow statement about swapping saturated fat for polyunsaturated fat and fewer cardiovascular events. Those sources are Hooper 2020 Cochrane (pub3), Mozaffarian 2010 and Jakobsen 2009, with Sacks 2017 as a position statement. They would not back any claim about mortality. Hamley 2017, which kept only adequately controlled trials and found no effect, and Steen 2026, where every pooled confidence interval crossed 1, show the trial evidence is genuinely contested. The supporting trial meta-analyses also draw on largely the same old trials, so they are not independent of each other.
evidence_gaps:
1. Re-run verification. At least 3 sources that all support the claim have to pass every check (identifier, metadata, peer review, not retracted, strong design, finding supported). The likeliest are Hooper 2020 pub3 (PMID 32827219; also check it is not the May 2020 pub2, PMID 32428300), Mozaffarian 2010 (PMID 20351774) and Jakobsen 2009 (PMID 19211817). Sacks 2017 may fail the strong-design check because it is a position statement.
2. Even after verification, independence is a concern. Hooper and Mozaffarian pool largely the same trials from the 1960s to 1990s, so a third source with a separate evidence base would make the case stronger. Jakobsen's cohorts could be that source, but they are observational. The verified 2026 AHA guidance (PMID 41914202) or a new large trial would also help.
3. Verify the contradicting and mixed sources (Hamley 2017, Steen 2026, Siri-Tarino 2010, Chowdhury 2014, de Souza 2015) and weigh them. This applies especially to Steen 2026, the most recent and largest risk-stratified review, whose existence and figures are unconfirmed. For Chowdhury 2014, check whether it has been corrected or retracted.
4. Resolve the disagreement over which trials to include (the Finnish Mental Hospital Study, Oslo, STARS, and the Minnesota Coronary Experiment re-analysis). It drives the difference between the positive analyses and the null ones.
5. Confirm the missing confidence intervals (Hooper pub3 mortality, the Steen stroke result, the Mozaffarian per-5%-of-energy estimate).
6. A verified primary source for any numeric intake cap, such as less than 10% of energy, before the app uses a threshold.

title: Ultra-processed food
statement: In meta-analyses of observational studies in adults, diets higher in ultra-processed foods (NOVA group 4) are associated with higher risk of several adverse outcomes. These include cardiovascular disease and death, death from any cause, type 2 diabetes, overweight and obesity, and depression or other common mental disorders. Certainty is mostly rated low or very low (one review rates type 2 diabetes as moderate). These studies show association, not cause, and they describe whole diets, not individual foods. Trial evidence is sparse and short-term. In one inpatient trial (20 adults, 2 weeks per diet), people ate about 500 kcal/day more on an ultra-processed diet than on an unprocessed diet matched for presented nutrients. In an 8-week trial in 55 adults, both diets followed healthy-eating guidance; weight fell on both, but less on the ultra-processed diet.
population: Adults in the prospective observational cohorts pooled by the meta-analyses. Ultra-processed food intake was classified with NOVA from reported diet. The Mendoza 2024 cohorts are US health professionals, and the reviews pool many of the same cohorts. Trial findings come from 20 weight-stable US adults on an inpatient ward (Hall 2019) and from 55 adults in England with BMI 25 to under 40 and high habitual ultra-processed food intake (Dicken 2025). Not established for children, pregnancy, individual foods or subgroups of ultra-processed foods.
what_the_app_does: Explains the processing line in food ratings. We describe processing; we never judge a food.
supporting_source_ids: src-lane-2024; src-dai-2024; src-pagliai-2021; src-mendoza-2024; src-hall-2019; src-dicken-2025; src-aramburu-2024
verdict: The status is active, for explanatory use only. Four counted observational syntheses agree that higher ultra-processed food intake is linked to worse outcomes: Lane 2024, Dai 2024, Pagliai 2021 and Mendoza 2024. Hall 2019 and Dicken 2025 support the trial description. However, the reviews pool overlapping cohorts, most certainty ratings are low or very low, and none can show cause. Aramburu 2024 found only 4 small, short randomised trials, with no significant effect for 30 of 42 outcomes. Dicken 2025 found that LDL cholesterol fell more on the ultra-processed diet. The 2025 US Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee review is not counted because it failed verification; it rated the evidence in children as only 'limited'. The statement therefore stays associative and says nothing about individual foods.
evidence_gaps:
1) Causal evidence is missing. Larger, longer randomised trials are needed that measure health outcomes, not just energy intake and weight, and that separate processing from nutrient content, energy density and palatability. The planned replication by Hall's group (NCT05290064) has no published results.
2) Observational exposure is weak. Cohorts that measure ultra-processed food intake better (repeated or objective measures rather than one self-report), and independent cohorts outside the US and Europe, would reduce the overlap between Lane, Dai, Pagliai and Mendoza.
3) Subgroup results are unverified. Mendoza 2024 subgroup hazard ratios (including the reported inverse links for bread/cold cereals and yoghurt/dairy desserts) need checking before the app says anything about types of ultra-processed food.
4) Some figures need checking before they can be cited: Pagliai 2021 all-cause mortality RR 1.25 and CVD RR 1.29, and the Lane 2024 effect sizes for anxiety and common mental disorders.
5) Identifier gaps: the PMID for Aramburu 2024, the PMCID for Hall 2019 and the standalone PubMed page for Mendoza 2024.
6) Children and pregnancy need peer-reviewed, verified evidence. The DGAC report graded the evidence in children as only limited and could not reach a conclusion for pregnancy.
7) The Matters Arising critiques of Dicken 2025, the authors' reply (PMID 41495410) and the BMJ rapid responses on Lane 2024's grading methods have not been read.

Status would move back to draft if a core source were retracted or corrected, or if a high-quality synthesis showed that the associations disappear after better adjustment or exposure measurement.
